title: Sets and Unique Values
learningObjectives: Explain a set as a collection that stores unique elements according to its equality rules.
Use set operations to add, remove, test membership, and eliminate duplicates.
Distinguish set membership from indexed access and sequence ordering.
Describe union, intersection, and difference at a basic level.
Recognize that equality and hashing rules affect which values count as duplicates.

understand.concept: A set is a collection designed to contain unique elements. Adding a value that is already present usually does not create a second copy. Sets are useful for membership checks and operations such as union, intersection, and difference. Most sets do not provide ordinary positional indexing, and ordering behavior varies by implementation.
understand.whyItMatters: Sets simplify tasks that require uniqueness—such as tags, seen identifiers, selected categories, or deduplicated data—and can provide efficient membership checks compared with searching some sequences.
understand.analogy: A guest list that records each person only once is like a set. If someone tries to add a name already on the list, the list does not gain a duplicate entry.
understand.analogyLimit: Uniqueness depends on the collection's equality and hashing rules. Some implementations preserve insertion order, others do not; sets should not be used when exact positional order is required.

explain.narrative: Use a set when duplicates are not meaningful and membership is important. Add, remove, and test elements with set operations. A union combines elements from either set; an intersection keeps elements shared by both; a difference keeps elements present in one set but not the other. For complex objects, understand which fields or identity rules determine uniqueness. If order matters, use a sequence or an ordered-set structure when available.

examples.explanation: Adding a new value increases the set; adding an existing value would not create a duplicate.

examples.title: Check membership
examples.explanation: Membership testing asks whether the value exists in the set.

examples.title: Remove an item
examples.explanation: The set removes the matching element, leaving other unique values.

examples.title: Union concept
examples.explanation: Union contains values present in either set, with duplicates eliminated.

commonMistakes: Using a set when the task requires position-based access or reliable order.
Assuming every set implementation has the same iteration order.
Misunderstanding how objects or composite values are compared for uniqueness.
Confusing union with intersection or difference.
